beats.narration_text: Merhaba — this is Liam, in for Bear. Episode 1 of 6. The assignment in one sentence: build a genuinely useful reallocation tool, then wrap it in the skeptical machinery that makes it trustworthy. Here is the one idea this series keeps returning to: a reallocation engine does not crash visibly. It produces a plausible answer to the wrong question — and then it moves the resource. Someone loses the staff, the capital, the credit, the aid. The six-episode arc: this episode, the shape of the danger, your domain, and the frictional prediction you write before you build. Episode 2, the working engine and the GIGO gate. Episode 3, the bias audit and the explanation that lies. Episode 4, Pearl's ladder — the fifteen-point heart of the whole thing. Episode 5, breaking your own build and the hard-stop gate. Episode 6, saying what the tool cannot know, and shipping. The build is the easy part. The doubting is the grade. Let's go.

beats.narration_text: What is a reallocation engine? Any system that decides to move a scarce resource from where it is to where it should be. Capital across a portfolio. Compute across jobs. Staff across shifts. Inventory across warehouses. Aid across regions. Attention across a feed. Credit across applicants. It ingests data, scores options, and outputs a move: take X from here, put it there. Why is that the single most dangerous shape an AI system can take? Two reasons, and they compound. First: it fails invisibly. A classifier that mislabels a photo is embarrassing. A reallocation engine that optimizes the wrong quantity produces a statistically valid recommendation on a causally incoherent claim — a chart that looks right, a number that holds up in review, a decision that quietly starves the wrong warehouse. Nothing crashes. Nothing throws an error. Second: it acts on the world. A classifier only labels. This thing moves the resource. Its errors are not abstract — they land on a person who loses the shift, the budget, the loan. Put those together and you get the exact failure this course is built to catch: a bias-amplifying reallocation deployed by someone with the skill to build it and the wrong framework to question it. The skill is cheap now. The framework is this assignment.

beats.act: pick your domain and your data
beats.narration_text: Pick one resource and one reallocation decision you can defend with domain knowledge. Six categories. Capital or budget — spend across campaigns or line items. Compute — jobs, cache, capacity across nodes. People and time — staff, shifts, reviewers. Inventory — stock, beds, bandwidth across sites. Attention — feed slots, recommendations, triage priority. Access — credit, aid, admissions, interventions across people. Note the warning on the last two: attention and access touch people's outcomes directly. Choose them and the bias audit and the hard-stop gate carry more weight — and so does your accountability for getting them right. Two more rules before you touch data. First, anchor your tool to a specific mechanism from The Reallocation Engine — the chapter and the page. Not the vibe of the book. A named mechanism you can point to. Second, the data rule: a real public dataset or a carefully documented synthetic one — and if synthetic, you must state what real-world structure it does and does not capture. Quality over volume. Two hundred clean, understood records beat two hundred thousand opaque ones. The dataset you fully understand is the only dataset you can interrogate — and interrogation is the entire second half of this rubric.

lines: One resource , one decision , defensible knowledge
Capital/budget , Compute , People/time , Inventory , Attention , Access.

beats.act: the frictional prediction and the tier split
beats.narration_text: Before you build anything, you write the frictional prediction. Timestamped, dated, before. Three things it must contain. One: what you expect the hardest failure to be — not a category like data quality, a specific expected failure in your specific domain. Two: how causally valid you expect the engine to turn out — will it be optimizing a real interventional quantity, or a correlation wearing a suit? Three: your confidence, as a number. Not 'fairly confident.' A number you can be wrong about. Immediately after you finish the project, you write the reflection: what actually happened, where the prediction missed, and what that says about your calibration. Miss either half and it is minus ten, automatically. Now the tier split, because it tells you where to spend your hours. The build is Tier 1 work — the tools are good at it, delegate freely. Let Claude draft the engine. The validation is Tier 4 and Tier 5 work: supervising the tool, formulating the right question, distinguishing correlation from causation, knowing when the output is wrong. That cannot be delegated, because it runs on your domain knowledge and your accountability. The rubric prices this honestly: the working tool is twelve points. The doubting is everything else.

beats.narration_text: Verdict for The Most Dangerous Shape and Pick Your Domain. A reallocation engine ingests data, scores options, and moves a scarce resource — and it is dangerous precisely because it fails invisibly and acts on the world at the same time. Pick one resource and one decision you can defend with real domain knowledge; if you choose attention or access, the stakes and the scrutiny both go up. Anchor to a named mechanism in the book — chapter and page. Choose data you fully understand, because interrogation is the second half of the rubric. And before any of it: the frictional prediction, timestamped — hardest expected failure, expected causal validity, confidence as a number. The build is Tier 1; delegate it. The validation is Tier 4 and 5; that part is you. Next episode: make the engine actually run, and make the data earn its way through the GIGO gate.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt to paste into Claude with your own answers filled in. The prompt reads: My domain is: one resource and one reallocation decision — for example, nurse shifts across hospital units, or ad spend across three campaigns. My dataset is: source, size, and time window. My book anchor is: the chapter and mechanism from The Reallocation Engine my tool implements. Draft my Frictional Journal prediction: the hardest failure I should expect, how causally valid the engine is likely to turn out, and my confidence as a number — present tense, first person, dated today. Why this prompt is worth running: Claude will draft a prediction that is plausible for your domain in general. Your job is to read it and find where it is generic — where it predicts what would go wrong for anyone, instead of what will go wrong for you, with your dataset, and your join, and your seasonality. Rewrite it in your own words, date it yourself, and commit it to the repo before you build. The gap between Claude's draft and what you actually believe is your first calibration reading — and it is the first thing in this assignment that cannot be delegated.
